name: Transistor Investment Payoff
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: From a Lab Curiosity to the Foundation of Modern Computing
lesson.summary: The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, took roughly a decade to become commercially competitive and far longer to reach its full economic impact, showing how even a genuinely working invention can require years of unglamorous engineering before the payoff arrives.
lesson.body:
In December 1947, physicists John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working under William Shockley at Bell Labs, built the first working point contact transistor, a small device that could amplify an electrical signal using a solid semiconductor crystal instead of a fragile, power hungry vacuum tube. Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. It is worth being honest that the original device was, by later standards, a mess: unreliable, hard to manufacture consistently, and initially outperformed by vacuum tubes in several practical respects. The invention crossed the bar described in the previous chapter, a real, demonstrated physical effect, but it was nowhere close to a finished commercial product.

The years that followed were spent on the unglamorous work of turning a laboratory effect into a manufacturable product. Shockley's later junction transistor design proved more practical to produce reliably than the original point contact device. Early commercial applications were modest: hearing aids, where the transistor's small size and low power draw mattered more than raw performance, and portable transistor radios in the mid 1950s, which introduced consumers to the idea that electronics could be small and battery powered. These were real products and real revenue, but they were not yet the economy reshaping impact the transistor is remembered for.

The larger payoff required additional inventions built on top of the original transistor. The integrated circuit, developed independently by Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in the late 1950s, showed how to put multiple transistors on a single chip, which solved reliability and wiring problems that had limited how complex a circuit could practically be. That, in turn, made possible the microprocessor, first commercialized by Intel in the early 1970s, which put an entire programmable computer's logic on one chip. Each of these steps took years of dedicated engineering and manufacturing investment on top of the last, and the transistor's full economic significance was not visible from 1947 alone. It emerged over roughly a quarter century of compounding follow on inventions.

The scale of the eventual payoff is difficult to overstate even with appropriate caution about specific figures, since exact numbers depend heavily on how the industry's boundaries are drawn and shift from year to year. What can be said with confidence is that the global semiconductor industry that grew from the transistor now measures its annual revenue in the hundreds of billions of dollars, and that transistors are now manufactured by the trillions annually across every category of consumer, industrial, and computing electronics, embedded in products that did not exist in any form in 1947. The lesson for a reader evaluating any speculative physics claim is not that every invention becomes the transistor, most do not, but that the transistor itself did not become an economic transformation on the day it was invented. It took roughly a decade to reach basic commercial viability and closer to a quarter century of further invention to reach the scale that makes it recognizable today as one of the most consequential technologies in history.
